world_behind.title: The classroom convenes
world_behind.text: For once the brothers come to Nephi with a question instead of a rod: "What meaneth these things which ye have read" (v. 1), framed in the era's live debate about prophecy: "according to the spirit and not the flesh" (v. 1) Their instinct to file Isaiah under "spiritual only" is the safe reading; safe readings ask nothing of the reader.

world_behind.title: The tribes already gone
world_behind.text: "the more part of all the tribes have been led away" (v. 4) states sober history: Assyria emptied the northern kingdom more than a century before Lehi left, and where those deportees went was unknown in Jerusalem then and after. The record's "whither they are none of us knoweth" (v. 4) is honest agnosticism, rare in any era's prophecy talk.

world_behind.title: A mighty nation, located
world_behind.text: Nephi reads Isaiah's nursing Gentiles as future history with an address: "a mighty nation among the Gentiles, yea, even upon the face of this land" (v. 7). The interpretation plants the fulfillment on his own hemisphere, which is why this record cares so much about what the Gentiles of this land eventually do with it.

world_behind.title: Malachi before Malachi
world_behind.text: The stubble that burns (v. 15) and the "calves of the stall" (v. 24) (v. 24) run word for word with Malachi 4:1–2, written well after Lehi's departure. Either the brass plates carried the older prophetic stock Malachi drew on, or the same Lord speaks the same sentences twice; the record, which later has Christ deliver Malachi entire (3 Ne. 24–25), never feels the difficulty it leaves us.

world_behind.title: A binding without chains
world_behind.text: Revelation chains the dragon for a thousand years; Nephi's mechanics are different: "because of the righteousness of his people, Satan has no power" (v. 26). The binding is demand-side: hearts in righteousness leave the tempter unemployed. Same millennium, but this record locates the padlock in the people.

world_behind.title: The editor's restraint
world_behind.text: "I durst not speak further as yet concerning these things" (v. 29): the same boundary drawn in the vision chapters (the sealed portions of ch. 14) governs the teacher's mouth. The small plates end their first book not because the material ran out but because the permission did.

words.text: Scattered "and be confounded" (v. 5): mixed past recognition, identity dissolved among the nations. The word is the scattering's real damage (losing not location but name), which is why the promise runs the other way in the same vocabulary: the righteous "are those who shall not be confounded" (v. 22).

words.text: "after they shall be nursed by the Gentiles" (v. 6): Isaiah's court image swallowed whole into Nephi's prose as a plain verb of history. Whole nations will do infant-care for scattered Israel, and the record has already made the word family its measure of power rightly used (21:23).

words.text: Gathered Israel comes "out of obscurity and out of darkness" (v. 12): not merely out of captivity but out of unnoticedness. Obscurity is the condition of the confounded, existing without being identified; the gathering's first gift is being known again, by the Lord and by themselves.

words.text: The old verb of checked daring: "I durst not speak further as yet" (v. 29). Nephi has used it for enemies afraid of him (17:52); turned on himself it marks reverence, not fear. The record's boldest teacher ends the book with the word for holding back.

phrases.text: The interpretive key, reused from the vision cycle: the liahona lesson was "things pertaining to things both temporal and spiritual" (v. 3) in figure (15:32); Isaiah is now read the same way. The record refuses the either/or its questioners offer; prophecy manifests by the Spirit and arrives "according to the flesh" (v. 2).

phrases.text: Zenos introduced the title (19:14); this chapter makes it the name of choice, six times, from the hardening against him to his millennial reign. Isaiah's favorite divine title becomes the interpretation's spine, and its climactic claim: Moses' prophet "was the Holy One of Israel" (v. 21).

phrases.term: a mighty nation among the Gentiles
phrases.text: The interpretation's boldest concrete prediction: a specific Gentile power "upon the face of this land" (v. 7), instrument of both scattering ("by them shall our seed be scattered" (v. 7)) and nursing (v. 8). The record holds both without contradiction: the same nation is rod and cradle, depending on the decade.

phrases.text: The vision's phrase (14:7) reappears with its audience widened: "not only unto the Gentiles but unto all the house of Israel" (v. 9). In chapter 14 it was set before the Gentiles as a choice; here it is the engine of the whole gathering, and the record itself is the work's advance copy.

phrases.term: saved, even if it so be as by fire
phrases.text: The preservation formula: "he will preserve the righteous by his power" (v. 17), even when the deliverance route runs through the flame that takes everything else. Paul will build the same figure (1 Cor. 3:15). Safety in this chapter is never exemption from the fire; it is ownership of what survives it.

phrases.text: The book's last instruction, and the formula's settled wording (13:37 said "unto"). After angels, visions, a compass, and a transoceanic ship, the closing requirement is unspectacular persistence: "if ye shall be obedient to the commandments, and endure to the end, ye shall be saved at the last day" (v. 31).

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The question, and the both-and
verses.text: The brothers propose "spiritual, not flesh"; Nephi answers with the record's standing rule: made known "by the voice of the Spirit" (v. 2), fulfilled "according to the flesh" (v. 2). Prophecy that stays spiritual asks for no repentance and predicts no history; Nephi's Isaiah does both.

verses.text: The tribes are already scattered to "the isles of the sea" (v. 4), the family among them, and the nursing prophecy is declared "temporal" (v. 6): "it meaneth us in the days to come" (v. 6). Likening stops being method and becomes address; the reading was never about someone else.

verses.label: v. 7–12
verses.title: The program of the gathering
verses.text: A mighty Gentile nation scatters, then nurses; a "marvelous work" (v. 8) goes out; Abraham's formula ("In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed" (v. 9)) is activated as the Lord makes "bare his arm in the eyes of the nations" (v. 10), and Israel comes "out of obscurity and out of darkness" (v. 12) knowing its Redeemer. Isaiah's poem is now an itinerary.

verses.label: v. 13–14
verses.title: The pit receives its diggers
verses.text: The great and abominable church drinks "drunken with their own blood" (v. 13), warring nations "shall fall into the pit which they digged to ensnare the people of the Lord" (v. 14): the vision's pit (14:3) filled exactly as promised. Evil in this record is not defeated so much as allowed to complete its own circle.

verses.label: v. 15–19
verses.title: Fire, sorted
verses.text: The proud burn "as stubble" (v. 15); the righteous are "saved, even if it so be as by fire" (v. 17), and twice the refrain: "the righteous need not fear" (v. 17). The same day is furnace or refining depending on what the fire finds; verse 18's blood and smoke fall on hearts hardened "against the Holy One of Israel" (v. 18), not on bystanders.

verses.label: v. 20–23
verses.title: The Prophet named, the kingdom taxed
verses.text: Moses' promised prophet (Deut. 18:15) is identified: "the Holy One of Israel" (v. 21), judge in righteousness. Against him stands the devil's kingdom, catalogued by business model: built up "to get gain" (v. 23), for "power over the flesh" (v. 23), for popularity, for lust. The taxonomy is the chapter's most quotable audit, and it measures institutions by their motives.

verses.label: v. 24–31
verses.title: The reign, and the close
verses.text: Calves of the stall, the Holy One reigning "in dominion, and might, and power, and great glory" (v. 24), one fold and one shepherd, Satan powerless "because of the righteousness of his people" (v. 26), and the book's widest door: all nations dwelling safely "if it so be that they will repent" (v. 28). Then Nephi stops at the boundary of permission and rests the whole book on one claim: the brass plates "are true" (v. 30), and their testimony is "that a man must be obedient to the commandments of God" (v. 30). Obedience, endurance, salvation: "And thus it is. Amen" (v. 31)

chapter.title: The discussion the reading was for
chapter.text: Two chapters of Isaiah end in a question-and-answer session, as the unit's design required: purpose (19), text (20–21), interpretation (22). The brothers ask Nephi rather than the Lord, as in chapter 15, but they ask, and the record rewards the question with its longest answer yet.

chapter.title: Temporal and spiritual, permanently
chapter.text: Nephi's both-and is the record's standing defense against two failure modes: prophecy spiritualized into harmlessness, and prophecy literalized into mere politics. Every later editor inherits the rule; covenant history is doctrine walking in the flesh.

chapter.title: The covenant arc, stated once, entire
chapter.text: Scattering for hardening; a Gentile nation as rod and then cradle; a marvelous work; the bared arm; gathering out of obscurity. This is the whole record's plot, laid out at the first book's close like an overture, and everything after it is enactment.

chapter.title: Judgment is self-service
chapter.text: Blood on their own heads, drunk on their own blood, swords of their own hands, the pit of their own digging: the chapter's destruction verbs are all reflexive. God's stated role is on the other ledger, preserving the righteous; the wicked are given only what they built.

chapter.title: Fear is assigned, not felt
chapter.text: "The righteous need not fear" twice, and one class that must: the catalogue of verse 23. The chapter treats fear as a fact about allegiance rather than temperament, which converts anxiety about the last days into a diagnostic question about the present ones.

chapter.title: The boldest identification
chapter.text: Pinning Deuteronomy's prophet-like-Moses on the Holy One of Israel is the interpretation's peak claim, the same one Peter will preach on the temple steps (Acts 3:22). The record's christology is not an addendum to the covenant story; it is the covenant story's subject.

chapter.title: A book ends on plainness
chapter.text: First Nephi closes not with the visions that filled it but with obedience and endurance, the two least glamorous words in its vocabulary. The colophon "And thus it is. Amen." seals a book whose argument has been, from the first verse's goodly parents, that the record is true and that truth asks something.

applications.title: Ask the meaning question
applications.text: The brothers' one great hour in this book begins with "What meaneth these things?" After your next reading, ask it out loud of one passage, and refuse the safe spiritual-only answer until you have also asked what it predicts, requires, or changes in the flesh.

applications.title: Read one prophecy as addressed mail
applications.text: Take a gathering or covenant promise and apply Nephi's "it meaneth us": write down what it means for your family line, your generation, your ward. Likening ends where "us" begins.

applications.title: Join the marvelous work at hand level
applications.text: The work of great worth runs on carried children and nursing strangers. Pick one concrete task this month (family history, a convert's first weeks, a returning member's dinner table) and be logistics for the gathering rather than audience.

applications.title: Run the verse 23 audit
applications.text: Gain, power over others, popularity, appetite: test your institutions and your own projects against the four builds. Anything that fails the audit belongs, by the chapter's taxonomy, to a kingdom with a short lease.

applications.title: Retire an assigned fear
applications.text: List what the last days currently cost you in dread, then read the refrain: the righteous need not fear. Move the energy from forecasting to allegiance; the chapter locates safety in whose you are, not in how well you predicted the fire.

applications.title: Bind Satan at household scale
applications.text: The millennium's mechanism, righteousness leaving the tempter powerless, does not wait for the millennium. Choose the one recurring temptation in your home and starve it structurally this week: no power because no purchase.

questions.text: When I ask what scripture means, am I hoping the answer stays spiritual, and what would a temporal answer require of me?
What part of my own family is currently "led away, and none of us knoweth whither," and what does this chapter promise about them?
Where in my life am I trusting that evil will simply fall into its own pit, and where am I called to do more than wait?
Which fire am I asking to be exempted from that God has only promised to bring me through?
Of the four builds (gain, power, popularity, appetite), which one funds my most respectable ambitions?
If my record ended today with one closing sentence, what would it testify that a man must do?
